newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African rebels want president out.
newsitem.headline: Central African rebels want president out.

text.p: Soldiers on a 10-day-old mutiny in Central African Republic called on Monday for the dismissal of President Ange-Felix Patasse, who is in France.
"He should never return to the country," declared rebel spokesman Sergeant Roger Kongbossomo after a round of churh-brokered talks to end the third mutiny in six months.
He said soldiers held Patasse guilty of "high treason".

"The president has introduced tribalism in the administration and army," Kongbossomo told Reuters. "He has distributed arms to his militants and entered alliances with foreign forces to the detriment of the national army."
Prime Minister Jean-Paul Ngoumpande acknowledged in a French radio interview that the situation in the country was serious but said the president's dismissal was not negotiable.

"I do not want to deny the seriousness of the situation, quite the contrary," Ngoumpande told Radio France Internationale. "We have a country which has chosen the path of democracy, a president who has been elected. Everything else can be negotiated, but not the dismissal of the head of state on the conditions set out -- and that is not negotiable."

Patasse survived a more serious army revolt over pay and status last May, but his future looks increasingly unclear. He has made no public statement on the latest crisis in the past week since he has been in France.

Ngoumpande said Patasse's stay in Paris had been delayed as he had to wait for French President Jacques Chirac to return from a visit to Japan. He had no clear answer when Patasse would return now that he had met with Chirac.
French troops based in the former French colony under bilateral accords helped quell the violent May mutiny that was followed by devastating looting in the capital.
They have been patrolling the capital since the soldiers revolted again on November 16, but appear to be avoiding any direct confrontation with the rebels.
Mutineers have gone about unhindered as they disarm members of a civilian militia loyal to Patasse.
Asked how soldiers would react if Patasse returned to Bangui under pressure from France, Kongbossomo said:
"If France wants to use all its might to tame Central African Republic it can go ahead...But the day France uses such force is the day we will set Bangui on fire," the sergeant said.
The government and mutineers began peace talks on Saturday, with the Roman Catholic Church mediating, but they appeared to be headed for stalemate over the latest rebel demand.
The capital was calm and banks and businesses opened normally with French troops still patrolling key points.

The army is divided between soldiers from Patasse's northern region and militants from the south, suspected of allegiance to former president Andre Kolingba, one of several candidates defeated by Patasse in multiparty elections in 1993.
The mutineers have also demanded pay from 1992 and 1993 and for Patasse to revoke a decree ordering a regiment involved in the pay revolts in April and May to a base out of the capital.
They also want implementation of recommendations made by a national conference after the May revolt, including forming a professional army with a greater role in national life.
France has reinforced its Bangui base from Chad. The French contingent in Bangui now numbers 1,500 men.
